older kernels have known bugs with RAID-5/6 and balance |\n36|\n37|## Quick Start\n38|\n39|```bash\n40|sudo apt install btrfs-progs\n41|sudo mkfs.btrfs -L mydata /dev/sdX1\n42|sudo mount /dev/sdX1 /mnt/mydata\n43|btrfs filesystem show /mnt/mydata\n44|btrfs device stats /mnt/mydata\n45|```\n46|\n47|## Key Operations\n48|\n49|| Task | Command |\n50||------|---------|\n51|| Show filesystems | `btrfs filesystem show` |\n52|| Filesystem usage (detailed) | `btrfs filesystem usage /mount` |\n53|| List subvolumes | `btrfs subvolume list /mount` |\n54|| Create subvolume | `btrfs subvolume create /mount/name` |\n55|| Delete subvolume | `btrfs subvolume delete /mount/name` |\n56|| Create read-write snapshot | `btrfs subvolume snapshot /mount/src /mount/dst` |\n57|| Create read-only snapshot | `btrfs subvolume snapshot -r /mount/src /mount/dst` |\n58|| Rollback: delete current, rename snapshot | `btrfs subvolume delete /mount/@; mv /mount/@snapshot /mount/@` |\n59|| Rollback: recreate subvolume from snapshot | `btrfs subvolume snapshot /mount/@snapshot /mount/@` |\n60|| Balance start (all chunks) | `btrfs balance start /mount` |\n61|| Balance start (metadata only) | `btrfs balance start -mconvert=raid1 /mount` |\n62|| Balance status | `btrfs balance status /mount` |\n63|| Balance cancel | `btrfs balance cancel /mount` |\n64|| Scrub start | `btrfs scrub start /mount` |\n65|| Scrub status | `btrfs scrub status /mount` |\n66|| Scrub cancel | `btrfs scrub cancel /mount` |\n67|| Check filesystem (read-only) | `btrfs check /dev/sdX` (unmounted) |\n68|| Defragment file or directory | `btrfs filesystem defragment -r /mount` |\n69|| Resize (grow) | `btrfs filesystem resize max /mount` |\n70|| Resize (shrink) | `btrfs filesystem resize -10G /mount` |\n71|| Add device | `btrfs device add /dev/sdY /mount` |\n72|| Remove device | `btrfs device remove /dev/sdY /mount` |\n73|| Device read/write error stats | `btrfs device stats /mount` |\n74|| Enable quotas | `btrfs quota enable /mount` |\n75|| Show qgroup usage | `btrfs qgroup show -reF /mount` |\n76|\n77|## Expected State\n78|\n79|- `btrfs device stats /mount` → all counters are `0` (any non-zero value is a read/write error)\n80|- `btrfs scrub status /mount` → `Status: finished` with `0 errors`\n81|- `btrfs balance status /mount` → `No balance found on \'/mount\'` when idle\n82|- `btrfs filesystem usage /mount` → Data and metadata ratios show reasonable allocation (metadata should not be >80% full)\n83|\n84|## Health Checks\n85|\n86|1. `btrfs device stats /mount` → all counters `0`; any non-zero value means hardware errors, act immediately\n87|2. `btrfs filesystem usage /mount` → check both Data and Metadata sections; metadata ENOSPC is the most common silent failure\n88|3. `btrfs scrub status /mount` → verify last scrub completed with no errors; schedule scrubs monthly via systemd timer or cron\n89|4. `btrfs subvolume list /mount` → audit snapshot count; accumulation fills disk without appearing in normal `df` output\n90|\n91|## Common Failures\n92|\n93|| Symptom | Cause | Fix |\n94||---------|-------|-----|\n95|| `no space left on device` but `df` shows free space | Metadata chunks exhausted while data chunks exist | `btrfs filesystem usage /mount` — run `btrfs balance start -dusage=50 /mount` to rebalance underused chunks |\n96|| RAID-1 on data but single on metadata | Dangerous default when adding a second disk; metadata is not redundant | `btrfs filesystem usage /mount` — check metadata profile; run `btrfs balance start -mconvert=raid1 /mount` |\n97|| Filesystem mounts read-only | Encountered an error it cannot self-correct | Check `dmesg | grep -i btrfs`; run `btrfs check /dev/sdX` on unmounted device to assess damage |\n98|| Balance fails with ENOSPC mid-run | Not enough free space to relocate all chunks | Use `-dusage=<N>` filter to relocate only partially-used chunks first; free up space before retrying |\n99|| Qgroup show reports inflated usage | Qgroups track snapshot references — shared data counted in each | Shared data is expected; use `btrfs qgroup show -reF` to see exclusive vs shared bytes |\n100|| Snapshot accumulation fills disk | Old snapshots reference deleted data, preventing space reclaim | `btrfs subvolume list /mount | grep snapshot` — delete old snapshots with `btrfs subvolume delete` |\n101|| `btrfs check --repair` made it worse | `--repair` is not safe for general use and can corrupt data | Never run `--repair` without consulting upstream; use `rescue` subcommands instead |\n102|| Filesystem errors after kernel upgrade | Older on-disk format or regression | Check `dmesg`; downgrade kernel or use `btrfs rescue` tools; check known issues for your kernel version |\n103|\n104|## Pain Points\n105|\n106|- **ENOSPC due to metadata/data imbalance**: The most common Btrfs "gotcha". Btrfs allocates space in chunks — if metadata chunks fill up, writes fail even when data chunks are available and `df` still shows free space. Fix: `btrfs balance start -dusage=50 /mount` to reclaim partially-empty chunks. This is not a bug — it is the expected behavior when chunk allocation becomes imbalanced.\n107|- **Mixed RAID profiles between data and metadata**: Adding a second disk does not automatically mirror metadata. A system can have `RAID1` data but `single` metadata, meaning metadata loss on one disk is fatal. Always explicitly set both with `-d` and `-m` flags.\n108|- **Snapshots are instant but they accumulate**: Snapshot creation is O(1) and free. Deletion requires reference counting and can be slow. Unreferenced snapshots hold on to deleted data indefinitely — disk usage only decreases after snapshot deletion completes.\n109|- **`btrfs check` is slow and `--repair` is risky**: Unlike `fsck.ext4`, Btrfs check does not have a safe repair mode. `--repair` can corrupt a filesystem that `check` reports as damaged. Prefer `btrfs rescue` subcommands (`zero-log`, `fix-device-size`) for targeted fixes.\n110|- **Btrfs RAID-5/6 has known parity issues**: As of kernels through 6.x, Btrfs RAID-5 and RAID-6 have unresolved write-hole bugs. Do not use RAID-5/6 for data you care about. Use RAID-1 or RAID-10 instead.\n111|- **Send/receive for backups**: `btrfs send` / `btrfs receive` is efficient for incremental backups using read-only snapshots as base references. Tools like `snapper` and `btrbk` automate the snapshot lifecycle and send/receive workflow — prefer them over manual scripting.\n112|- **CoW fragmentation on databases and VMs**: Copy-on-write writes new data to new locations, which fragments sequential files over time. Use `nodatacow` mount option (or `chattr +C`) for VM disk images, database files, and other large randomly-written files. `nodatacow` also disables checksums for those files.\n113|\n114|## See Also\n115|\n116|- **ext4** — Traditional Linux filesystem without CoW overhead; use when you need maximum compatibility and don\'t need snapshots\n117|- **xfs** — High-performance filesystem for large sequential I/O; use for databases and media workloads where CoW fragmentation is a concern\n118|- **zfs** — Full storage stack with pooling and replication; use when you need enterprise-grade checksums and send/receive without kernel version sensitivity\n119|- **lvm** — Logical volume manager; provides snapshot and resize capabilities at the block layer beneath btrfs\n120|\n121|## References\n122|\n123|See `references/` for:\n124|- `btrfs-options.md` — mkfs and mount options organized by category\n125|- `common-patterns.md` — filesystem setup, subvolume layouts, snapshots, rollback, backup, RAID, and compression\n126|- `docs.md` — official documentation and community links', 'total_lines': 126, 'file_size': 8377, 'truncated': False, 'is_binary': False, 'is_image': False, 'not_found': False}

{'content': '1|---\n2|name: rust-memory-optimization\n3|description: |\n4|  Memory optimization and allocation reduction in Rust. Use when:\n5|  - User is designing memory-sensitive or low-latency systems\n6|  - Optimizing data structures to reduce memory footprint\n7|  - Replacing heap allocations with stack-allocated/bounded structures (SmallVec, ArrayVec, ThinVec)\n8|  - Handling small strings with optimizations (CompactString)\n9|  - Reusing collections via clear() in loops\n10|  - Implementing zero-copy decoding and references\n11|  - Structuring arena-allocated memory (Bumpalo)\n12|  - Measuring memory usage, profiling heap, or diagnosing leaks\n13|---\n14|\n15|\n16|\n17|## Quick Navigation\n18|\n19|- [references/stack_allocations.md](references/stack_allocations.md)\n20|- [references/arenas.md](references/arenas.md)\n21|\n22|# Rust Memory Optimization Guide\n23|\n24|Advanced strategies for reducing allocations, shrinking layout sizes, and boosting performance.\n25|\n26|## Core Rules & Patterns\n27|\n28|### 1. Bounded Heap-Free Collections\n29|For collections that are usually small, avoid standard vectors to bypass heap allocations.\n30|- **`SmallVec`**: Stack-allocated up to a threshold, overflows to the heap.\n31|- **`ArrayVec`**: Fixed-capacity array wrapper; never allocates on the heap.\n32|- **`ThinVec`**: Only takes a single pointer size when empty, reducing size in enum layouts.\n33|\n34|```rust\n35|use smallvec::{smallvec, SmallVec};\n36|use arrayvec::ArrayVec;\n37|\n38|// SmallVec: Allocates 4 items on the stack. Goes to heap only if count > 4.\n39|let mut local_tags: SmallVec<[String; 4]> = smallvec![];\n40|local_tags.push("Rust".to_string());\n41|\n42|// ArrayVec: Absolute limit of 8 items on the stack. No heap overflow.\n43|let mut coordinates: ArrayVec<f64, 8> = ArrayVec::new();\n44|coordinates.push(42.0);\n45|```\n46|\n47|### 2. Small String Optimization (SSO)\n48|Standard `String` consumes 24 bytes and allocates heap space immediately. Use `CompactString` for inline small strings (under 24 bytes) without allocating.\n49|\n50|```rust\n51|use compact_str::CompactString;\n52|\n53|// No heap allocation for strings <= 24 characters\n54|let username = CompactString::new("user_123");\n55|```\n56|\n57|### 3. Boxed Slices vs Vectors\n58|If a collection\'s size is determined once at initialization and never changes, convert it from `Vec<T>` to `Box<[T]>` to save 8 bytes of stack capacity space.\n59|\n60|```rust\n61|let items_vec: Vec<i32> = vec![1, 2, 3];\n62|\n63|// Save capacity field (shrinks stack representation from 24 to 16 bytes)\n64|let items_slice: Box<[i32]> = items_vec.into_boxed_slice();\n65|```\n66|\n67|### 4. Zero-Copy Patterns\n68|Instead of cloning or allocating strings, hold references to existing memory using slices or crates like `bytes::Bytes`.\n69|\n70|```rust\n71|use bytes::Bytes;\n72|\n73|pub struct Message {\n74|    // Zero-copy reference-counted byte buffer slice\n75|    pub payload: Bytes,\n76|}\n77|\n78|// Can be sliced and shared among threads without cloning underlying memory\n79|let original = Bytes::from(vec![0; 1024]);\n80|let slice = original.slice(0..100); \n81|```\n82|\n83|### 5. Arena Allocation\n84|For batch allocation where structures share a lifecycle (e.g. AST parsing), use arena allocators (`bumpalo`) to allocate items sequentially in a continuous region of memory and free them all at once.\n85|\n86|```rust\n87|use bumpalo::Bump;\n88|\n89|let bump = Bump::new();\n90|\n91|// Allocates quickly on the bump arena\n92|let string_ref = bump.alloc_str("dynamic string");\n93|let int_ref = bump.alloc(42);\n94|\n95|// Entire arena is cleared at once on drop\n96|```\n97|\n98|### 6. Collection Reuse\n99|Reuse collection allocations in performance-critical loops with `.clear()` instead of re-instantiating.\n100|\n101|```rust\n102|// Bad: Allocates a new vector every iteration\n103|for item in feed {\n104|    let mut batch = Vec::new();\n105|    batch.push(item);\n106|}\n107|\n108|// Good: Reuses allocation buffer\n109|let mut batch = Vec::with_capacity(100);\n110|for item in feed {\n111|    batch.clear();\n112|    batch.push(item);\n113|}\n114|```\n115|\n116|## Layout Awareness\n117|\n118|Use `std::mem::size_of` to understand data layout.\n119|\n120|```rust\n121|println!("User size: {}", std::mem::size_of::<User>());\n122|```\n123|\n124|Reorder fields to reduce padding only when the type is numerous or hot.\n125|\n126|```rust\n127|// Often smaller: group large-alignment fields first\n128|struct Record {\n129|    id: u64,\n130|    flags: u32,\n131|    kind: u8,\n132|}\n133|```\n134|\n135|## String Strategy\n136|\n137|```rust\n138|fn label<\'a>(name: &\'a str, fallback: &\'a str) -> std::borrow::Cow<\'a, str> {\n139|    if name.is_empty() { fallback.into() } else { name.into() }\n140|}\n141|```\n142|\n143|Avoid `format!` in tight loops. Reuse buffers with `clear()`.\n144|\n145|## Zero-Copy Parsing\n146|\n147|Return slices into the input when the input outlives parsed data.\n148|\n149|```rust\n150|pub struct Header<\'a> {\n151|    pub name: &\'a str,\n152|    pub value: &\'a str,\n153|}\n154|```\n155|\n156|Do not force zero-copy when it creates unmanageable lifetimes for little gain.\n157|\n158|## ThinVec for Enum Payloads\n159|\n160|When enums contain `Vec` variants, `ThinVec` reduces the enum size by storing only a pointer when empty:\n161|\n162|```rust\n163|use thin_vec::ThinVec;\n164|\n165|// Regular Vec in an enum makes the enum 24+ bytes even when empty\n166|enum Node {\n167|    Leaf(i64),\n168|    Children(Vec<Node>),     // 24 bytes for Vec\n169|}\n170|\n171|// ThinVec only stores 8 bytes (a pointer) when empty\n172|enum NodeOptimized {\n173|    Leaf(i64),\n174|    Children(ThinVec<Node>), // 8 bytes for ThinVec\n175|}\n176|```\n177|\n178|## Cow for Conditional Ownership\n179|\n180|```rust\n181|use std::borrow::Cow;\n182|\n183|pub struct Error {\n184|    message: Cow<\'static, str>,\n185|}\n186|\n187|impl Error {\n188|    // No allocation for static messages\n189|    pub fn new(msg: &\'static str) -> Self {\n190|        Self { message: Cow::Borrowed(msg) }\n191|    }\n192|\n193|    // Allocates only when dynamic\n194|    pub fn with_detail(msg: String) -> Self {\n195|        Self { message: Cow::Owned(msg) }\n196|    }\n197|}\n198|```\n199|\n200|## Arc vs Rc Trade-offs\n201|\n202|```rust\n203|use std::rc::Rc;\n204|use std::sync::Arc;\n205|\n206|// Single-threaded shared ownership — cheaper than Arc\n207|let shared = Rc::new(large_data);\n208|\n209|// Multi-threaded shared ownership — required across threads\n210|let shared = Arc::new(large_data);\n211|```\n212|\n213|Prefer `Rc` when data never crosses thread boundaries. `Arc` adds atomic reference counting overhead.\n214|\n215|## HashMap Memory Optimization\n216|\n217|```rust\n218|use hashbrown::HashMap;\n219|\n220|// hashbrown\'s HashMap uses less memory than std\'s and is faster\n221|let mut map: HashMap<String, i32> = HashMap::with_capacity(128);\n222|\n223|// Reserve capacity upfront to avoid rehashing\n224|map.reserve(expected_count);\n225|\n226|// Consider FxHashMap for non-adversarial keys\n227|use rustc_hash::FxHashMap;\n228|let mut fast_map: FxHashMap<String, i32> = FxHashMap::default();\n229|```\n230|\n231|## Stack vs Heap Decision Matrix\n232|\n233|| Type | Stack Size | Heap Alloc | Use When |\n234||------|-----------|------------|----------|\n235|| `String` | 24 bytes | Yes | Owns mutable text |\n236|| `&str` | 16 bytes | No | Borrowed text, lifetime bound |\n237|| `CompactString` | 24 bytes | No (≤24 chars) | Short strings that own data |\n238|| `Cow<str>` | 32 bytes | Conditionally | Mostly static, rarely dynamic |\n239|| `Box<str>` | 16 bytes | Yes | Owned fixed string |\n240|| `Vec<T>` | 24 bytes | Yes | Growable collection |\n241|| `SmallVec<[T; N]>` | ~24+ bytes | Only if >N | Usually small, occasionally large |\n242|| `Box<[T]>` | 16 bytes | Yes | Fixed-size after construction |\n243|| `ThinVec<T>` | 8 bytes | Only if non-empty | Empty or small in enums |\n244|\n245|## Measuring Memory\n246|\n247|```rust\n248|use std::alloc::{GlobalAlloc, System, Layout};\n249|\n250|struct TrackingAllocator;\n251|\n252|unsafe impl GlobalAlloc for TrackingAllocator {\n253|    unsafe fn alloc(&self, layout: Layout) -> *mut u8 {\n254|        System.alloc(layout)\n255|    }\n256|\n257|    unsafe fn dealloc(&self, ptr: *mut u8, layout: Layout) {\n258|        System.dealloc(ptr, layout)\n259|    }\n260|}\n261|\n262|// For detailed profiling, use dhat, heaptrack, or valgrind\n263|```\n264|\n265|Use `dhat` crate for heap profiling in tests:\n266|\n267|```rust\n268|#[cfg(test)]\n269|mod tests {\n270|    #[test]\n271|    fn memory_test() {\n272|        let _profiler = dhat::Profiler::new_heap();\n273|        // code under test\n274|        // dhat prints allocation stats on drop\n275|    }\n276|}\n277|```\n278|\n279|## Optimization Workflow\n280|\n281|1. Measure allocations and CPU first.\n282|2. Identify the hot path and expected data sizes.\n283|3. Pick the narrowest memory change.\n284|4. Benchmark before/after.\n285|5. Keep readability unless the win is meaningful.\n286|\n287|## Allocation Decision Rules\n288|\n289|- `Vec<T>`: general purpose growable collection.\n290|- `SmallVec<[T; N]>`: usually-small collection with occasional heap spill.\n291|- `ArrayVec<T, N>`: hard maximum size, no heap allocation.\n292|- `Box<[T]>`: fixed-size heap slice after construction.\n293|- `Bytes`: shared immutable byte buffers.\n294|- `Bump`: many same-lifetime allocations.\n295|- `Cow<\'a, T>`: borrow unless mutation/ownership is required.\n296|\n297|## Anti-Patterns\n298|\n299|```rust\n300|// Bad: cloning a large Vec just to avoid lifetime complexity\n301|let data = original.clone(); // expensive and unnecessary\n302|\n303|// Good: use Arc or Cow for shared ownership\n304|let data: Arc<[u8]> = original.into();\n305|```\n306|\n307|```rust\n308|// Bad: allocating inside a hot loop\n309|for item in items {\n310|    let s = format!("processing {}", item); // allocates every iteration\n311|}\n312|\n313|// Good: reuse a buffer\n314|let mut buf = String::with_capacity(128);\n315|for item in items {\n316|    buf.clear();\n317|    write!(buf, "processing {}", item).unwrap();\n318|}\n319|```\n320|\n321|- Replacing every `Vec` with `SmallVec` without measuring.\n322|- Keeping arena references after reset.\n323|- Cloning strings to satisfy ownership instead of shortening borrow scopes.\n324|- Using `Arc` as a default clone workaround.\n325|- Optimizing layout for types created a handful of times.\n326|- Using `Box<dyn Trait>` when generics would eliminate the allocation entirely.\n327|\n328|## Review Prompt\n329|\n330|When reviewing memory optimization, ask what was measured, which allocation is removed, what lifetime assumptions changed, and whether the new type increases stack size or API complexity.\n331|\n332|## Optimization Checklist\n333|\n334|- Measure allocations before changing data structures.\n335|- Preallocate collections only when capacity is known or bounded.\n336|- Prefer borrowing and `Cow` before cloning strings or buffers.\n337|- Use arenas only when lifetimes are truly batch-scoped.\n338|- Check stack growth when replacing heap allocations with inline storage.\n339|- Re-benchmark after changes and keep the simpler version if gains are noise.\n340|- Profile with `dhat` or `heaptrack` to find actual allocation hotspots.\n341|- Consider `hashbrown` or `rustc-hash` for HashMap-heavy code.\n342|\n343|## References\n344|\n345|- [Rust Performance Book: Heap Allocations](https://nnethercote.github.io/perf-book/heap-allocations.html)\n346|- [smallvec](https://docs.rs/smallvec)\n347|- [arrayvec](https://docs.rs/arrayvec)\n348|- [bumpalo](https://docs.rs/bumpalo)\n349|- [compact_str](https://docs.rs/compact_str)\n350|- [bytes](https://docs.rs/bytes)\n351|- [dhat](https://docs.rs/dhat)\n352|- Use when writing safe systems code, managing resources, or preventing memory bugs.\n4|---\n5|\n6|# Memory Safety Patterns\n7|\n8|Cross-language patterns for memory-safe programming including RAII, ownership, smart pointers, and resource management.\n9|\n10|## When to Use This Skill\n11|\n12|- Writing memory-safe systems code\n13|- Managing resources (files, sockets, memory)\n14|- Preventing use-after-free and leaks\n15|- Implementing RAII patterns\n16|- Choosing between languages for safety\n17|- Debugging memory issues\n18|\n19|## Core Concepts\n20|\n21|### 1. 45|## Agent operating contract
46|
47|### Scope and execution
48|- Identify the requested outcome, affected components, and evidence needed
49|  to show completion before editing.
50|- Maintain one shared task with clear file ownership when delegating.
51|  Subagents inherit the same scope and permission limits.
52|- Complete authorized work autonomously. Do not ask permission for routine
53|  reads, isolated tests, reversible edits, or implementation choices.
54|- Follow demonstrated dependencies. Do not expand a repair into unrelated
55|  refactoring, new infrastructure, or speculative optimization.
56|- When new evidence expands the scope, state why and update the task.
57|
58|### Identity, permissions, and grants
59|- Use the identity and supported control-plane entry point assigned to
60|  the task. Preserve caller identity through delegated work.
61|- Existing authorization persists; do not ask for the same approval twice.
62|- A denied operation is evidence of a permission boundary. Record the
63|  operation, caller, exact missing capability or policy, and error.
64|- Do not bypass a denial through another identity, direct database edits,
65|  alternate transports, or privileged host commands.
66|- Do not broaden grants, weaken autonomy/security policies, expose secrets,
67|  or change unrelated identities to make a task pass.
68|- If a permission change is necessary, first prepare the smallest concrete
69|  change: affected principal, capability, resource scope, duration, expected
70|  effect, verification, and rollback. Request approval only for the part
71|  not already explicitly authorized.

73|### Evidence and verification
74|- Distinguish proposed, implemented, tested, and deployed work.
75|- Verify the complete affected workflow, including failure and cancellation
76|  paths where relevant. A successful component test is not end-to-end proof.
77|- Use disposable fixtures and bounded workloads. Preserve authoritative
78|  data and unrelated work.
79|- Report failed or unavailable checks honestly. Do not convert missing
80|  coverage into a pass or repeatedly run unchanged failing checks.
81|- Prefer the smallest evidence-backed fix. Add technology only when a
82|  measured problem justifies its complexity.

85|- Sync decisions, conversations, and tool results to the shared repository
86|  with agent identity, timestamps, task ID, and source references.
87|- Use NotebookLM to recover context. Verify current code, permissions,
88|  configuration, and deployment state against their authoritative sources.
89|- Record the current commit, modified files, validation results, unresolved
90|  blockers, and exact next action. Update stale conclusions explicitly.
91|- Never describe planned work or another agent's claim as completed work.
92|
93|### Completion
94|- Finish with the outcome, changes, verification, remaining limitations,
95|  and deployment status.
96|- Stop when the requested outcome is verified; do not continue into
97|  speculative optimization or unrelated cleanup.

120|cross target or the Codex executable's own musl packaging does not change the

Note: `/usr/local/bin/systemctl` on this host is a shim that returns plausible answers — using it masks the deprecation; always use `sv`. Do not use `systemctl` or other foreign service-manager CLIs. Container/app deployment uses D-Bus via `busctl`.

138|## Deployment (btrfs send/receive)
139|
140|**Owner clarification (2026-09-13): there is no deployment script. Deployment
141|is btrfs send/receive of the prepared filesystem snapshot.** The release
142|boundary is the snapshot's contents and the send/receive transfer. Existing
143|`deploy/` scripts are source/history or preparation tooling; neither
144|`build-golden.sh` nor `btrfs-layout.sh` defines the current deployment mechanism.
145|Never hand-copy binaries onto a running host as a deploy step.
146|
147|**Owner decision (2026-10-14): `./activate-golden.sh` at the repo root is the one
148|command for deploying a new version.** It runs the internal
149|`deploy/lib/golden/build-golden.sh` helper, then `op-release-launch release`:
150|btrfs send/receive of a golden snapshot into the inactive of two slots, then a
151|live read-only overlay swap at `/opt/op-dbus/current` (active + previous only;
152|`op-release-launch rollback` undoes it). The 2026-09-13 "no deployment script"
153|rule above is superseded for this entry point; the transport is still send/receive.
154|
155|`deploy/lib/golden/build-golden.sh` only populates and validates
156|`/opt/op-dbus/golden` from already built artifacts and an already sealed,
157|persisted catalog. Set `OP_PERSISTED_CATALOG_SOURCE` to use an isolated release
158|catalog; the script validates and copies it but never reseals it. It does not
159|create the read-only release snapshot, send
160|or receive it, activate a received filesystem, install files into the running
161|host, or restart services. `--golden-only` remains a compatibility alias for
162|its default behavior; the former `--live-only` and `--no-restart` modes are
163|retired. Snapshot creation, `btrfs send/receive`, target activation, and any
164|deliberate target service action are separate operator steps.
165|
166|```sh
167|CXXFLAGS="-include cstdint" cargo build --workspace --release
168|sudo target/release/opblob seal-shm            # explicitly reseal after the build
169|sudo target/release/opblob persist             # retain the catalog across reboot
170|```
171|
172|After builds, explicitly run the freshly built `opblob` to seal the release catalog; bridge startup only consumes sealed blobs and never reseals. For isolated release preparation, use `seal-plugins <new-catalog-dir>` and pass that catalog as `OP_PERSISTED_CATALOG_SOURCE`; publishing live SHM remains part of activation. Match the service's schema-shaping environment. The renamed cognitive code reads `COGNITIVE_*`: `COGNITIVE_QDRANT_URL` defaults to `http://127.0.0.1:6334`, matching the current `deploy/runit/op-grpc-bridge/run`; the historical `COGNITIVE_MCP_QDRANT_URL=http://10.200.0.2:6334` instruction is obsolete. After an explicit GNU-target build, use `target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/release/opblob`, not an older default-target artifact. Verify the live and persisted catalogs match after activation. Review catalog removals and keep a recoverable copy before a full reseal, which sweeps plugin IDs absent from the build.
173|
174|The commands above describe build/catalog preparation, not deployment. Do not
175|infer a live install or restart from a successful build or snapshot preparation.

177|**Clean-baseline activation (2026-09-22):** local releases are received under
178|`/opt/op-dbus/releases/<release-id>` and selected by the atomic
179|`/opt/op-dbus/current` symlink. The operator procedure and rollback contract

184|8084; the duplicate `zeroclaw` service name is retired. This defines the

188|
189|The workspace has **37 member crates under `crates/`, plus the root `op-dbus`

299|## Architecture — the load-bearing invariants (read these before touching plugins, state, or identity)
300|
301|- **Identity storage lifecycle (owner correction 2026-10-05).** Cozo owns identity-to-leaf/loop assignment and isolation. One immutable physical seed is shared through read-only views; each identity keeps its own writable leaf and the existing seven subvolumes. Only the external host provisioner may add a new blank leaf once, during explicit creation. Login, start, stop, logout, restart, bridge recovery and failed-start cleanup must NEVER add/remove Btrfs members. Start verifies/remounts the existing pair through the host mount owner; stop leaves membership and data intact. The bridge only verifies externally mounted storage and records logical attachment. Do not interpret `attached=false` as device removal. No root copies, snapshots, new subvolumes or OverlayFS fallback during identity provisioning. Never modify a seed while retained leaves depend on it. Older add-on-start/remove-on-stop guidance in source, handoffs and signals is superseded; do not restore it. Host release snapshot/send/receive below is a separate deployment mechanism.
302|- **D-Bus is the only control plane.** Every plugin is a D-Bus object at `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/<name>` under `org.opdbus.v1`. No `Command::new(...)` subprocesses, no direct file reads for live state, no polling loops in plugin/service code. New backend capabilities register as plugins in `crates/op-plugins/src/default_registry.rs` — never as new gRPC proto service packages.
303|- **The plugin IS the schema — one source of truth, nonnegotiable.** That single schema is sealed into the blob, which IS the plugin. D-Bus method signatures, MCP tool inputs, gRPC shapes, and UI field renderers derive from it. Validate inputs against it. Each plugin defines its schema under `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/`, using `plugin_scaffold_helpers.rs`. **There must be no parallel plugin schema source in a repository-level or plugin `schemas/` directory.** The former plugin capture directories, separate section files, and JSON-file loader have been removed. `crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/schema_loader.rs` still exists by name, but it reads only a manifest-pinned `PluginSchema` from the sealed blob catalog; it is not a file-schema fallback. **Owner correction (2026-10-18): capture threetched's full `config schema` from the verified binary on every seal.** The shared capture fixes the runtime config directory, checks the binary and manifest, and supplies native_config, MCP, model_routes, plugins and skill_bundles. `tched_router_contract.rs` contains only access/section helpers; the embedded UPSTREAM IMPORT is retired. Build-time generated bridge contracts explicitly prepare the same capture; runtime consumes the sealed catalog and never starts capture as a fallback. Do not restore an embedded schema or add independent captures using the sealer's ambient environment. The per-section generator and generated surface were retired on 2026-10-04. Older docs claiming a single `plugin_schema_defs.rs` are also stale — that file does not exist.
304|- **The sealed blob IS the plugin.** Present state lives in the sealed blob catalog at `/dev/shm/opdbus/plugin-blobs/<plugin_id>.<schema_hash16>.blob`. A plugin exists ⟺ its blob is in the catalog. The sole writer is the blob sealer in `op-blob`. Consumers read SHM directly (zero-copy) — they never re-hash and never consult the Rust registry for existence. The old `/dev/shm/opdbus/schemas` folder and `live-schema.json` are gone.
305|- **MutationEngine owns state; streaming comes from SHM (owner reaffirmed 2026-09-13).** MutationEngine folds authoritative backend results into the complete state tree, including child objects, and commits that state to canonical SHM before change notifications. Child updates/deletions must preserve unrelated children and parent fields. Existing subscriptions derive their values from committed SHM; an in-memory event payload, method argument, or generator buffer is not a second state authority. Preserve verified principal/session scope for private state. Do not add a separate per-method streaming control plane or claim a buffered unary response provides state streaming.
306|- **MCP gateway (settled).** One public MCP door: `:8090` on `op-grpc-bridge` (cognitive MCP is in-process there; no standalone `op-cognitive-mcp` runit service). `compact_mcp` is a retired plugin id. Compact *mode* (4 meta-tools) is in-process in op-web for the singleton control-plane chatbot; it is not an MCP plugin and not a second listener. Never create new shims or point external clients at `op-assistant-grpc`.
307|- **External binaries back plugins; the plugin remains the single schema source.** 3tched-router / tched-router (`tched_router` in code) is the framework/schema/plugin integration backed by the autonomous `/usr/bin/threetched` executable. The reproducible threetched input is pinned in `vendor/tched-router/source.pin`; `vendor/tched-router/build-threetched.sh` applies the checked-in patches and emits `target/threetched-artifacts/tched-router/{threetched,manifest.json}` without installing it. `build-golden.sh` validates the pin, patch and binary provenance, then stages the binary, `/usr/share/op-dbus/threetched-manifests/tched-router.json`, `/etc/op-dbus/threetched-runtime.toml`, and the tracked default skill bundle into the golden filesystem. The `tched-router` runit service verifies that manifest, exact commit, binary digest, and version before exec, then seeds its private runtime config and skills from those staged bootstrap files. A fresh checkout includes the digest-pinned upstream source archive, patches and build recipe; the helper verifies and uses that archive by default. Cargo registry dependencies and system build tools still need provisioning. Owner correction (2026-10-11): the executable and runtime-facing branding are lowercase `threetched`; the FUSE discovery source is `threetched-surface.rs`. Preserve upstream repository URLs, licenses and historical provenance. The former instruction to keep the executable named zeroclaw is superseded. The plugin contract remains `tched_router_contract.rs`, and source attribution may identify `zeroclaw config schema`.
308|- **Owner-confirmed lifecycle and model roles (2026-09-13, reaffirmed 2026-09-14).** Waypipe is retired: its crate directory, Cargo membership, binary target and protocol are absent; `retired-binaries`/`retired-services` prevent stale build or service artifacts from entering golden. Do not restore it in source exports or release inputs. Assistant is the control-plane chatbot, not an `assistant` container. The historical Gemma routing role is model agnostic; the `op-gemma` crate is retired (2026-09-19: directory, Cargo membership and binary removed, listed in `retired-binaries`) — the `gemma_brain` plugin remains and its role does not constrain the model/provider. Cargo membership and legacy names do not establish active deployments.
309|- **Factory role correction (2026-09-14).** The former Factory account/platform plugin is retired from the registry and dispatch. The intended access is CLI/SSH; routing belongs to `tched_router`, and Factory billing requires an actual native binding. Provider names or relabelled direct upstream routes do not prove that binding. A future Missions integration needs its own verified native contract; do not restore the retired REST platform methods from historical fixtures or docs.
310|- **Standalone vendor adapters are retired (2026-09-14).** The `op-grpc-adapters` crate directory and its `op.adapters.v1` protocol are absent after Netmaker retirement. Its duplicate mail/MQ services bypassed canonical plugin admission. Do not restore this crate or its old Netmaker clients. The existing bridge `operation.mail.v1` service and retained EMQX plugin are separate surfaces; their presence does not prove every mail or MQTT method is implemented.
311|- **Identity minting and metadata (owner reaffirmed 2026-09-13).** The identity subsystem owns minting the identity and its SealedId/SID1 credential blob. This is distinct from an OPBLOB01 plugin blob and does not belong in the plugin catalog. Clients forward the authored credential through the transport's identity metadata; they do not mint or reconstruct it from genesis/trace/key headers. Verify minting, persistence, injection and receiver validation as separate links. Current source assigns session/SID1 creation to MutationEngine with the op-identity format; the existence of an HTTP/MCP helper does not prove every gRPC client injects SID1.
312|- **Identity injection (owner decision 2026-09-25).** The decoy mints the sealed identity blob; the 8090 interceptor anchors the session and writes the identity metadata (`anchor_verified_human_session` and `insert_identity_metadata` in `crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/interceptor.rs`). The oracle (OIA1) is the decoy's signed peer proof; the human credential (SID1) is the session identity for that key. The bridge's own client and MutationEngine are the wrong place for session or identity injection. Source and live state did not match this on 2026-09-25: the interceptor still mints genesis server-side when no session exists (`mint_and_store_genesis` in `anchor_verified_human_session`), and the decoy issuer mints only OIA1. Transport paths (decoy, WARP, door addresses) are in `docs/src/operations/network.md`.
313|- **Btrfs storage and transport (owner correction 2026-09-23).** Deployment remains the prepared snapshot transferred by `btrfs send/receive`. The earlier global five-subvolume limit and instruction to replace Snowball/cache subvolumes with ordinary directories are withdrawn. Preserve the original `operation-dbus-proto` cache/NUMA/timing architecture: Btrfs cache category subvolumes; authoritative timing plus vector/state subvolumes; aligned read-only snapshot sets and send/receive. See the original repo `branding/product-baseline.md` §12 and `crates/op-snowball/{DESIGN,REQUIREMENTS}.md` (R5). Retention is configurable per storage owner, not a global five-subvolume cap. Parent snapshots do not include nested subvolume contents: snapshot and transport every required member explicitly. Never flatten existing subvolumes or delete historical data to satisfy the withdrawn limit. Preserve security, writer-locking, identity and error-handling fixes while correcting storage regressions.
314|- **No SQLite — use CozoDB.** CozoDB (`op-cozo-store`) is the embedded database for this project. Do not add new `rusqlite` or other SQLite use. `op-cache/src/btrfs_cache.rs` already uses a Cozo index; current `workstack_cache.rs`, `workflow_cache.rs`, `workflow_tracker.rs`, and `pattern_tracker.rs` still use `rusqlite` and remain migration debt rather than an approved pattern.
315|- **RAG pipeline and Voyage-4 models.** Live source file indexing goes through `code_index` (mode='source') into Qdrant collections: `repos_lsp_*_voyage_4_large` and `repos_lsp_*_voyage_4_lite`. Voyage-4 models are interchangeable across their dimension (1024 for all variants); `_large` and `_lite` refer to model size/quality tier, not embedding space. All collections share a single fused retrieval space and can be queried together. Legacy `repos_lsp_*_voyage_code_4` collections and `repomix_rag` collection are retired — do not use them. The standalone `notebooklm-mcp` service is retired; the plugin-owned `notebooklm` contract and bridge provider remain. Owner reaffirmed NotebookLM conversation/tool-history sync on 2026-10-05; use its declared methods through identity-bound 3tchedFS. Do not confuse this corpus sync with the Voyage source-indexing pipeline.
316|
317|## Handoff between agents
318|
319|Claude, Codex, Grok and any other agent share one handoff: `HANDOFF.md`. Read it
320|at the start of every session, after this file. Claim your task in its *Active
321|work* table before changing anything, and never reset, stash or overwrite work
322|another agent has claimed there. Before the session ends, or before a context or
323|usage limit, update your row and add a dated *Handoff* entry. A handoff kept only
324|in one agent's private memory is invisible to the others, so it does not count.
325|
326|## Signals and task board
327|
328|- **Append observations to `SIGNALS.md`** rather than letting them evaporate in chat. Three signal types: `💡 SUGGESTION` · `⚠️ CONCERN` · `👁️ OBSERVATION`. Each row: date · model · signal · optional `→ OD-##` link. Models leave status `open`. Promote anything actionable to `WISHLIST.md` as an `OD-##` and link it back.
329|- **`WISHLIST.md` is the canonical task board** — do not create new TODO docs. Priority buckets: Critical/Urgent → Current → Next → Future → When I Have Staff. Dispatch syntax: "dispatch <ID> to <agent>" spawns an agent with the task context and updates status here.
330|- **Read recent `SIGNALS.md` rows before non-trivial work** in the area they touch — the file records load-bearing gotchas (stale vendored deps, live/deployed drift, the live-vs-intent identity topology) that source alone will not surface.
331|
332|## Stale documentation
333|
334|- **README.md is stale**: crate count (31) is wrong, `cd lovable` is a deleted directory, `sudo service6` references are retired. Prefer AGENTS.md and source over README claims.
335|- Many older deploy scripts and HANDOFF docs still reference s6 — treat them as archival; runit/`sv` is current.
336|- Anything mentioning `/dev/shm/plugin_schema.dat`, `live-schema.json`, or `/dev/shm/opdbus/schemas` is describing a retired design.
337|- Anything mentioning `OIB1`, `oib1:`, `blob_ref`, `SessionIdentityBlob`, or `x-opdbus-identity-blob-bin` is pre-2026-09-01 and stale; the session-identity envelope is now `SID1` / `SealedId`.
338|- Anything referencing `crates/op-web/ui/`, `zeroclaw-gui`, pairing codes, or `operation-dashboard-ui-07` — the production UI is `/srv/git/3tched.com` (github.com/repr0bated/3tched.com), deployed from that repo through `scripts/publish-op-web.sh`. `LANDING` selects the mount name; `URL_PREFIX=/` selects the dashboard root.
339|- Older deployment-script and backup/restore hierarchy descriptions are not current deployment authority. Deployment is btrfs send/receive of the prepared snapshot — see architecture invariants above.
340|
341|## Subagent and model selection
342|
343|Cargo execution follows JEV routing above; the guidance below does not allocate
344|Cargo models.
345|
346|**Owner preference (2026-09-13, model names withdrawn 2026-09-24,
347|reaffirmed 2026-09-30): assess task
348|difficulty and required reasoning before delegation, and use the cheapest
349|available model that can complete it at the same quality.** A lower price must
350|not thin the answer, skip evidence, or weaken a judgment. If the cheaper model
351|would lose accuracy, completeness, or care, use the more capable model. Pick
352|from the models the session can actually launch. Do not inherit an expensive
353|parent model by default, and do not pin a product or model id in this file.
354|Use a low-cost model for lookups, inventory extraction, documentation
355|assembly and routine non-Cargo checks when that model can match the
356|quality of a more capable one. Choose low effort for mechanical work and
357|medium effort for bounded reasoning. Escalate when the task's quality needs
358|it or a cheaper attempt falls short, and briefly state why.
359|
360|Keep the primary agent available for user communication and coordination.
361|Delegate longer execution and research jobs, use nonblocking progress checks,
362|and avoid long blocking tool calls on the primary. User messages steer active
363|work; answer them promptly while delegated work continues. Small immediate
364|edits and decisions can remain with the primary when delegation would add
365|overhead.
366|
367|For non-Cargo delegation, choose the appropriate agent role:
368|
369|- `Explore` (fast read-only) for locating code, grepping symbols, answering "where is X."
370|- `Plan` for architecture and design before writing code.
371|- `general-purpose` only when the task needs multi-step reasoning or execution that Explore or Plan cannot cover.
372|- Use a more capable model for complex cross-crate reasoning, security review, or ambiguous architectural decisions, and for any standard edit, build fix, or test whose quality would drop on the low-cost agent.

2|name: ovs-db-analysis
3|description: >-
4|  Analyze Open vSwitch data from sosreport — conf.db, OpenFlow dumps, port stats,
5|  tunnels, and datapath health. Use when troubleshooting OVS packet drops, flow
6|  performance, bridge/port/interface issues, DPDK vs kernel datapath, or when the
7|  user mentions sosreport openvswitch, ovs-ofctl, ovsdb-tool, or ovs-db-analysis.
8|---
9|
10|# OVS Database and Flow Analysis
11|
12|This skill provides detailed analysis of Open vSwitch (OVS) data collected via sosreport. It operates in four modes:
13|
14|1. **Default mode**: Full analysis - conf.db + all text files (requires ovsdb-tool, falls back to text files if not available)
15|2. **Database mode (`--db`)**: Database only - analyze conf.db (requires ovsdb-tool)
16|3. **Text files mode (`--flows-only`)**: Text files only - no ovsdb-tool needed
17|4. **Query mode (`--query`)**: Run custom OVSDB JSON queries (requires ovsdb-tool)
18|
19|## When to Use This Skill
20|
21|Use this skill when:
22|- **Troubleshooting packet drops** - Find drop flows being hit
23|- **Analyzing flow performance** - View top flows by packet count
24|- Analyzing OVS configuration from a sosreport
25|- Troubleshooting bridge, port, or interface issues
26|- Investigating DPDK vs kernelspace datapath
27|- Reviewing tunnel configurations (VXLAN, Geneve, GRE)
28|- Checking port statistics (drops, errors, traffic)
29|- Mapping Kubernetes pods to OVS interfaces
30|
31|## Prerequisites
32|
33|**Default mode** (full analysis):
34|- **ovsdb-tool** must be installed (from openvswitch package)
35|- Falls back to `--flows-only` if ovsdb-tool not found
36|- Sosreport with `sos_commands/openvswitch/` directory and `conf.db`
37|
38|**Database mode** (`--db`):
39|- **ovsdb-tool** must be installed (from openvswitch package)
40|  - Check: `which ovsdb-tool`
41|  - Fedora/RHEL: `sudo dnf install openvswitch`
42|  - Ubuntu/Debian: `sudo apt install openvswitch-common`
43|- Sosreport with `conf.db` file
44|
45|**Text files mode** (`--flows-only`):
46|- No special tools needed - works out of the box!
47|- Sosreport with `sos_commands/openvswitch/` directory
48|
49|**Query mode** (`--query`):
50|- **ovsdb-tool** must be installed
51|- Incompatible with `--flows-only`
52|
53|## File Locations in Sosreport
54|
55|The sosreport collects:
56|```
57|sosreport-hostname-date/
58|├── etc/openvswitch/conf.db              (OVS database - for --db mode)
59|├── var/lib/openvswitch/conf.db          (alternate location)
60|└── sos_commands/openvswitch/            (default mode uses these)
61|    ├── ovs-vsctl_-t_5_show              (topology)
62|    ├── ovs-vsctl_-t_5_list_bridge       (bridge details)
63|    ├── ovs-vsctl_-t_5_list_interface    (interface details)
64|    ├── ovs-vsctl_-t_5_list_Open_vSwitch (system info)
65|    ├── ovs-ofctl_dump-flows_<bridge>    (OpenFlow entries)
66|    ├── ovs-ofctl_dump-ports_<bridge>    (Port statistics)
67|    ├── ovs-appctl_coverage.show         (internal stats)
68|    ├── ovs-appctl_upcall.show           (datapath health)
69|    ├── ovs-appctl_tnl.ports.show_-v     (tunnel ports)
70|    └── ...
71|```
72|
73|## Analysis Script
74|
75|The analysis script is located at:
76|```
77|<plugin-root>/skills/ovs-db-analysis/scripts/analyze_ovs_db.py
78|```
79|
80|## Implementation Steps
81|
82|### Step 1: Locate the Analysis Script
83|
84|```bash
85|SCRIPT_PATH=$(find ~ -name "analyze_ovs_db.py" -path "*/sosreport/skills/ovs-db-analysis/scripts/*" 2>/dev/null | head -1)
86|
87|if [ -z "$SCRIPT_PATH" ]; then
88|    echo "ERROR: analyze_ovs_db.py script not found."
89|    exit 1
90|fi
91|```
92|
93|### Step 2: Run the Analysis
94|
95|```bash
96|# Default: Full analysis - conf.db + text files (requires ovsdb-tool)
97|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport-hostname-date/
98|
99|# Analyze from archive
100|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport-hostname-date.tar.xz
101|
102|# Database only mode (requires ovsdb-tool)
103|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/ --db
104|
105|# Text files only mode (no ovsdb-tool needed)
106|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/ --flows-only
107|```
108|
109|### Step 3: Custom Queries (Optional, requires --db)
110|
111|For specific investigations, use raw OVSDB queries:
112|
113|```bash
114|# Query all bridges
115|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/ --query '["Open_vSwitch", {"op":"select", "table":"Bridge", "where":[], "columns":["name","datapath_type","fail_mode"]}]'
116|
117|# Query VXLAN interfaces
118|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/ --query '["Open_vSwitch", {"op":"select", "table":"Interface", "where":[["type","==","vxlan"]], "columns":["name","options"]}]'
119|
120|# Query interfaces with errors
121|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/ --query '["Open_vSwitch", {"op":"select", "table":"Interface", "where":[], "columns":["name","error"]}]'
122|```
123|
124|## Analysis Output
125|
126|The default mode analyzes:
127|
128|| Analysis | Source File | Description |
129||----------|-------------|-------------|
130|| System Info | `ovs-vsctl_-t_5_list_Open_vSwitch` | OVS/DPDK version, system type, external IDs |
131|| Topology | `ovs-vsctl_-t_5_show` | Bridge overview with ports grouped by type |
132|| Bridge Details | `ovs-vsctl_-t_5_list_bridge` | Datapath type, fail mode, CT zones |
133|| Interfaces | `ovs-vsctl_-t_5_list_interface` | By type, pod interfaces with mapping |
134|| OpenFlow | `ovs-ofctl_dump-flows_*` | Flow counts, drops, top flows |
135|| Port Stats | `ovs-ofctl_dump-ports_*` | RX/TX drops and errors |
136|| Tunnels | `ovs-appctl_tnl.ports.show_-v` | Configured tunnel ports |
137|| Datapath Health | `ovs-appctl_upcall.show` | Flow table usage vs limit |
138|| OVS Stats | `ovs-appctl_coverage.show` | Internal counters (netlink, OVSDB, etc.) |
139|
140|## OpenFlow Analysis Features
141|
142|| Feature | Description |
143||---------|-------------|
144|| Flow Count | Total flows per bridge (total, drop, with hits) |
145|| Drop Detection | Flows with `actions=drop` that have packet hits |
146|| Top Flows | Most active flows sorted by n_packets |
147|| Table Distribution | Flow counts per OpenFlow table |
148|| Port Drops | RX/TX drop counters per port |
149|| Port Errors | RX/TX error counters per port |
150|| Datapath Health | Flow table usage vs limit (from upcall.show) |
151|| OVS Stats | Internal statistics (netlink, OpenFlow, OVSDB transactions) |
152|
153|## OVN Internal Tables (Ignore Drops in These)
154|
155|When analyzing drop flows in OVN-managed bridges (br-int), **ignore drops in table 44 and tables 64-87** as these are internal OVN mechanics, not security policy or real packet drops.
156|
157|> **⚠️ Note:** OVN and OVS are complex systems and table mappings can change between releases. Always verify drop analysis against the specific OVN version in use. When in doubt, check the OVN source code for your release.
158|
159|| Table | Name | Purpose |
160||-------|------|---------|
161|| **44** | **CHK_LB_OUTPUT** | **Loopback prevention - drops packets that would loop back (high volume, normal)** |
162|| 64 | SAVE_INPORT | Save ingress port for later |
163|| 65 | LOG_TO_PHY | Logical to physical mapping |
164|| 66 | MAC_BINDING | MAC binding lookups |
165|| 67 | MAC_LOOKUP | MAC address table lookups |
166|| 68-69 | CHK_LB_HAIRPIN | Load balancer hairpin checks |
167|| 70 | CT_SNAT_HAIRPIN | Conntrack SNAT hairpin |
168|| 71-72 | GET/LOOKUP_FDB | FDB (forwarding DB) lookups |
169|| 73-74 | CHK_IN_PORT_SEC | Ingress port security |
170|| 75 | CHK_OUT_PORT_SEC | Egress port security |
171|| 76-77 | ECMP_NH | ECMP next-hop handling |
172|| 78 | CHK_LB_AFFINITY | Load balancer affinity |
173|| **79** | **MAC_CACHE_USE** | **MAC cache miss (high volume, normal)** |
174|| 80 | CT_ZONE_LOOKUP | Conntrack zone lookup |
175|| 81-83 | CT_ORIG_*_LOAD | Conntrack original tuple loading |
176|| 84 | FLOOD_REMOTE_CHASSIS | Remote chassis flooding |
177|| 85 | CT_STATE_SAVE | Conntrack state save |
178|| 86 | CT_ORIG_PROTO_LOAD | Conntrack protocol loading |
179|| 87 | GET_REMOTE_FDB | Remote FDB lookup |
180|
181|**Relevant drop tables for troubleshooting:**
182|- **Table 9**: Ingress ACLs - actual policy drops (look for `reg0=0x8000`)
183|- **Table 0**: Initial classification drops
184|- **Tables < 64**: Generally meaningful drops
185|
186|## Common Analysis Scenarios
187|
188|### 1. Troubleshooting Packet Drops
189|
190|```bash
191|# Quick analysis (default mode, no ovsdb-tool)
192|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/
193|```
194|
195|Look for:
196|- **ACTIVE DROP FLOWS** section showing flows dropping packets
197|- **PORT STATISTICS** showing ports with drops/errors
198|
199|### 2. Checking DPDK Configuration
200|
201|```bash
202|# Default mode shows DPDK info from text files
203|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/
204|
205|# Or use database mode for custom queries
206|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/ --query '["Open_vSwitch", {"op":"select", "table":"Open_vSwitch", "where":[], "columns":["dpdk_initialized","other_config"]}]'
207|```
208|
209|### 3. Investigating Pod Connectivity
210|
211|The interface analysis shows pod-to-OVS mapping:
212|- Interfaces with `external_ids` containing `iface-id`
213|- Interface names ending with `_h` (veth host side)
214|
215|### 4. Datapath Health Check
216|
217|The upcall stats show:
218|```
219|DATAPATH FLOW TABLE HEALTH
220|  Current flows: 155 / 200,000 (0.1% used)
221|  Average: 156, Max seen: 215
222|  ✓ Flow table healthy
223|```
224|
225|If usage > 90%, flows are being evicted too aggressively.

2|name: kernel-fuse-diagnosis
3|description: >
4|  FUSE（用户态文件系统）内核端故障诊断技能。当用户提到 FUSE 文件系统 hang、
5|  所有操作返回 EIO、FUSE daemon 崩溃/重启、请求队列阻塞、D 状态进程堆积、
6|  /sys/fs/fuse/connections/ 异常、libfuse 兼容性、max_read/max_write 配置不当、
7|  writeback cache 一致性问题、多线程 FUSE daemon 死锁、容器中 /dev/fuse 权限问题、
8|  FUSE 性能退化等关键词时，必须使用本技能。
9|  覆盖场景：FUSE daemon 崩溃后 EIO、请求队列阻塞与 D 状态、max_read/max_write 配置不当、
10|  writeback cache 一致性问题、多线程 daemon 死锁、/dev/fuse 权限问题、内核 FUSE 模块 Bug、
11|  混合复杂 FUSE 故障。即使只收到"文件系统挂了"、"目录打不开"、"ls 卡死"但挂载点
12|  为 FUSE 类型时也应触发本技能。
13|  支持 FUSE 全链路诊断（sysfs 队列 → 内核参数 → daemon 进程 → 代码级根因）。
14|---
15|
16|# FUSE 内核端故障诊断（三层下钻：系统层 → 类型层 → 代码根因层）
17|
18|## 第一节：故障目录结构
19|
20|```text
21|fuse_case/                  # 故障案例目录
22|├── scripts/                # 【内置】本技能的诊断脚本
23|│   ├── 01_baseline_info.sh
24|│   ├── branch_A_daemon_crash.sh
25|│   ├── branch_B_req_queue.sh
26|│   ├── branch_C_max_read_write.sh
27|│   ├── branch_D_writeback_cache.sh
28|│   ├── branch_E_mt_deadlock.sh
29|│   ├── branch_F_dev_fuse_perm.sh
30|│   ├── branch_G_kernel_bug.sh
31|│   └── branch_H_mixed.sh
32|├── logs/                   # 【可选】应用日志
33|│   ├── application.log

35|├── fuse_state/             # 【可选】故障时刻的 FUSE 状态快照
36|│   ├── connections.txt     # ls /sys/fs/fuse/connections/
37|│   ├── waiting.txt         # cat .../waiting

48|
49|## 第二节：分析策略（三层下钻，逐层收敛）
50|
51|FUSE 内核端故障诊断采用**三层下钻模型**，从最外层逐层深入，层间存在依赖关系：
52|
53|```
54|┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
55|│                   三层下钻分析模型                                 │
56|│                                                                 │
57|│   L1: 系统层         mount -t fuse /proc/mounts                 │
58|│       │               /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*                │
59|│       └─ 判断：FUSE 挂载点是否正常？连接是否存在？               │
60|│                                                                 │
61|│   L2: 类型层         strace -p <daemon_pid>                     │
62|│       │               cat /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/waiting     │
63|│       └─ 判断：是 EIO？请求阻塞？性能退化？权限问题？            │
64|│                                                                 │
65|│   L3: 代码/内核层    FUSE daemon 源码分析                       │
66|│                      内核 FUSE 模块参数 (/sys/module/fuse/)     │
67|│                      /dev/fuse 设备状态                          │
68|│                      └─ 根因定位：daemon 崩溃 / 队列阻塞 / 配置  │
69|│                                                                 │
70|│   每层输出：证据 + 结论。L3 输出最终根因。                       │
71|└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
72|```
73|
74|### 故障分类树
75|
76|```
77|L1 ─ FUSE 挂载点与连接检查
78|│
79|├─ L2 ─ 挂载点正常？─────── 否 ──→ 非 FUSE 问题，转其他技能
80|│                         是
81|│                         ↓
82|├─ L2 ─ 操作返回 EIO？──── 是 ──→ Branch A (Daemon Crash)
83|│                         否
84|│                         ↓
85|├─ L2 ─ 进程 D 状态/Hang？ 是 ──→ Branch B (Req Queue) / Branch E (MT Deadlock)
86|│                         否
87|│                         ↓
88|├─ L2 ─ 性能退化？─────── 是 ──→ Branch C (Max Read/Write)
89|│                         否
90|│                         ↓
91|├─ L2 ─ 数据一致性异常？─ 是 ──→ Branch D (Writeback Cache)
92|│                         否
93|│                         ↓
94|├─ L2 ─ 权限问题？─────── 是 ──→ Branch F (dev/fuse Perm)
95|│                         否
96|│                         ↓
97|├─ L2 ─ 内核崩溃/Oops？── 是 ──→ Branch G (Kernel Bug)
98|│                         否
99|│                         ↓
100|└─ L2 ─ 混合/复杂现象？── 是 ──→ Branch H (Mixed)
101|```
102|
103|---
104|
105|## 第三节：诊断流程
106|
107|### L1: 系统层 — 基线采集与挂载点检查
108|
109|检查系统 FUSE 基础配置与挂载状态，判断是否为系统级配置问题。
110|
111|```bash
112|# 1. 检查 FUSE 挂载点
113|mount -t fuse
114|
115|# 2. 检查 /proc/mounts 中 FUSE 条目
116|grep fuse /proc/mounts
117|
118|# 3. 检查 FUSE 内核连接状态
119|ls /sys/fs/fuse/connections/ 2>/dev/null
120|
121|# 4. 检查 FUSE daemon 进程
122|ps aux | grep -E "[f]use|[F]ILESYSTEM_NAME"
123|
124|# 5. 基本连通性测试
125|ls -la <FUSE_mount_point>
126|stat <FUSE_mount_point>/test_file 2>&1
127|```
128|
129|**L1 结论判定**：
130|
131|| 现象 | 可能原因 | 下一层 |
132||------|---------|--------|
133|| 挂载点 ls 返回 EIO | FUSE daemon 崩溃 | Branch A |
134|| ls 卡死/D 状态 | 请求队列阻塞 | Branch B |
135|| 性能异常慢 | max_read/max_write 配置不当 | Branch C |
136|| 数据不一致 | writeback cache 问题 | Branch D |
137|| daemon 进程存在但无响应 | 多线程死锁 | Branch E |
138|| 权限 denied | /dev/fuse 权限 | Branch F |
139|| 内核 Panic/Oops | FUSE 内核模块 Bug | Branch G |
140|| 多种现象共存 | 混合故障 | Branch H |
141|
142|### L2 → L3: 类型层与代码根因层
143|
144|#### Branch A — FUSE Daemon 崩溃后 EIO
145|
146|**触发条件**：L1 中访问 FUSE 挂载点返回 "Transport endpoint is not connected" 或 EIO。
147|
148|```
149|L2 诊断：
150|├── 1. stat <mount_point>（确认 EIO 错误码）
151|├── 2. grep <mount_point> /proc/mounts（挂载条目是否仍存在）
152|├── 3. ls /sys/fs/fuse/connections/（连接是否已销毁）
153|├── 4. ps aux | grep <daemon_name>（daemon 进程是否存在）
154|├── 5. journalctl -u <daemon_service> --since "5 min ago"（daemon 退出日志）
155|├── 6. dmesg | grep -i fuse（内核 FUSE 消息）
156|├── 7. cat /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/abort 2>/dev/null（abort 状态）
157|│
158|└── L3 根因判定：
159|    ├── daemon 进程不存在 + 连接已销毁 → daemon 崩溃/被 OOM Kill
160|    ├── daemon 进程不存在 + 连接残留 → daemon 退出但连接未清理
161|    ├── daemon 存在但连接状态异常 → daemon 内部状态机错误
162|    ├── dmesg 显示 "fuse: aborting connection" → 内核主动中止
163|    ├── OOM Killer 日志 → daemon 因内存超限被内核杀死
164|    └── 连接 abort 状态为 1 → 手动触发 abort 或 daemon 调用 abort
165|```
166|
167|**典型输出**：
168|```
169|结论: FUSE daemon 进程不存在（已崩溃），
170|      /sys/fs/fuse/connections/ 目录为空（连接已销毁）。
171|      dmesg 无 FUSE 相关错误，但 journalctl 显示 daemon 因
172|      SIGSEGV (signal 11) 退出。
173|根因: FUSE daemon 程序存在内存访问越界 Bug，导致段错误崩溃。
174|```
175|
176|#### Branch B — FUSE 请求队列阻塞
177|
178|**触发条件**：LS 卡死、进程 D 状态（uninterruptible sleep）、`/sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/waiting` 持续增长。
179|
180|```
181|L2 诊断：
182|├── 1. cat /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/waiting（请求队列深度）
183|├── 2. cat /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/max_background（最大后台请求数）
184|├── 3. ps aux | grep D | grep -v grep（D 状态进程列表）
185|├── 4. cat /proc/<D_pid>/stack（查看 D 状态内核栈）
186|├── 5. strace -e trace=write,read,ioctl -p <daemon_pid>（daemon 系统调用）
187|├── 6. cat /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/congested_threshold_ms（拥塞阈值）
188|├── 7. dmesg | grep -i "fuse.*block"（阻塞告警）
189|│
190|└── L3 根因判定：
191|    ├── waiting 持续增长 + daemon 未处理请求 → daemon 侧线程阻塞
192|    ├── daemon 进程 strace 显示 read() 未被唤醒 → 内核/FUSE 调度问题
193|    ├── D 状态进程内核栈显示 fuse_request_send → 请求队列已满等待
194|    ├── max_background 设置过小 → 请求队列排队上限低导致积压
195|    ├── daemon write() 变慢或阻塞 → daemon 后端存储 I/O 瓶颈
196|    └── congested_threshold 触发 → FUSE 内核主动限流
197|```
198|
199|**典型输出**：
200|```
201|结论: /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/waiting 持续增长（当前值: 512），
202|      进程 D 状态栈显示 fuse_request_send。
203|      strace 显示 daemon read() 调用未被及时唤醒。
204|根因: FUSE daemon 工作线程池太小或线程卡在后端 I/O 上，
205|      无法及时消费内核下发的 FUSE 请求。
206|```
207|
208|#### Branch C — max_read/max_write 配置不当
209|
210|**触发条件**：FUSE 文件系统性能显著低于预期，小文件/大文件读写性能异常。
211|
212|```
213|L2 诊断：
214|├── 1. cat /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/max_read（当前 FUSE 最大读取大小）
215|├── 2. cat /sys/module/fuse/parameters/max_read（内核模块参数）
216|├── 3. mount | grep <fuse_type>（挂载参数 -o max_read=,max_write=）
217|├── 4. dd if=<mount_point>/test of=/dev/null bs=1M count=100（读性能测试）
218|├── 5. dd if=/dev/zero of=<mount_point>/test bs=1M count=100（写性能测试）
219|├── 6. iostat -x 1 <device>（底层 I/O 延迟）
220|├── 7. strace -e pread64,pwrite64 -p <daemon_pid>（系统调用大小对比）
221|│
222|└── L3 根因判定：
223|    ├── max_read=4096（4K）→ 每次读请求仅传输 4K，大文件读性能极差
224|    ├── max_write=4096（4K）→ 每次写请求仅传输 4K，写性能瓶颈
225|    ├── max_read 与底层存储块大小不匹配 → 产生大量小 I/O
226|    ├── 挂载时未指定 max_read= → 使用默认值（通常 1MB，但某些 FUSE 缩减）
227|    ├── daemon 未实现 readdir 缓存 → 目录遍历性能退化
228|    └── 内核 max_read 参数被 sysfs 限制 → 无法超过内核模块设置的上限
229|```
230|
231|**典型输出**：
232|```
233|结论: max_read=4096（4K），远低于默认 1MB。
234|      dd 读测试仅 12 MB/s，远低于预期 200+ MB/s。
235|      strace 确认每次 pread64 仅传输 4096 字节。
236|根因: FUSE 挂载时未指定 max_read，daemon 初始化协商值为 4K
237|      （libfuse 旧版本默认），导致大文件顺序读性能退化。
238|```
239|
240|#### Branch D — Writeback Cache 一致性问题
241|
242|**触发条件**：FUSE 文件系统写入后读取数据不一致、写入顺序错误、重复内容。
243|
244|```
245|L2 诊断：
246|├── 1. mount | grep <fuse_type> | grep -o "writeback_cache"（检查是否启用）
247|├── 2. cat /sys/module/fuse/parameters/use_writeback_cache（内核参数）
248|├── 3. echo "test" > <mount_point>/file && cat <mount_point>/file（一致性测试）
249|├── 4. strace -e write,pwrite64,fsync -p <daemon_pid>（跟踪写操作时序）
250|├── 5. dd if=/dev/urandom of=<mount_point>/test bs=4K count=100（并发写入）
251|├── 6. md5sum <mount_point>/test && sleep 1 && md5sum <mount_point>/test（变化检测）
252|├── 7. grep -i "fuse.*invalidate" /proc/<daemon_pid>/stack（缓存无效化状态）
253|│
254|└── L3 根因判定：
255|    ├── writeback_cache 启用但 daemon 未实现 ->release 回调 → 数据未刷入后端
256|    ├── 并发写入后的读取返回过期数据 → page cache 未正确无效化
257|    ├── daemon write() 返回成功但数据未持久化 → 缺少 fsync 语义
258|    ├── 内核 fuse_conn 中 writeback_cache=1 但后端不支持原子写
259|    ├── mmap 写入后数据丢失 → FUSE 不支持 shared mmap writeback cache
260|    └── multi-page writeback 顺序错误 → daemon 未按 LBA 顺序处理请求
261|```
262|
263|**典型输出**：
264|```
265|结论: writeback_cache 启用后，写入 100 个 4K 块后的 md5sum
266|      在不同读取时间点返回不同值。
267|      daemon 未实现 ->write() 回调的完整 writeback 语义。
268|根因: FUSE daemon 启用 writeback_cache 模式但未正确处理
269|      内核的 writeback 请求，page cache 与后端存储数据不一致。
270|```
271|
272|#### Branch E — 多线程 FUSE Daemon 死锁
273|
274|**触发条件**：FUSE daemon 进程存在但操作挂起，挂载点操作无响应。
275|
276|```
277|L2 诊断：
278|├── 1. ps -eLf | grep <daemon_name>（daemon 线程列表）
279|├── 2. cat /proc/<daemon_pid>/stack（主线程内核栈）
280|├── 3. for tid in $(ls /proc/<daemon_pid>/task/); do echo "TID:$tid"; cat /proc/$tid/stack 2>/dev/null; done
281|├── 4. strace -f -e trace=write,read,ioctl -p <daemon_pid>（多线程追踪）
282|├── 5. gdb -p <daemon_pid> -batch -ex "thread apply all bt"（全线程回溯）
283|├── 6. cat /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/waiting（确认请求堆积）
284|├── 7. kill -USR1 <daemon_pid>（向 daemon 发送信号检查状态）
285|│
286|└── L3 根因判定：
287|    ├── 所有工作线程在 pthread_mutex_lock 等待 → 互斥锁死锁
288|    ├── 线程 A 持有锁 L1 等待锁 L2，线程 B 持有锁 L2 等待锁 L1 → 经典死锁
289|    ├── 工作线程在 write() 后端存储时阻塞 → I/O 死锁（等待自身填充）
290|    ├── 线程池所有线程都在 fuse_session_process 中 → 请求循环依赖
291|    ├── 主线程在 fuse_loop 中阻塞但工作线程已退出 → 线程管理 Bug
292|    └── daemon 中 fuse_reply_* 调用顺序错误 → 协议级死锁
293|```
294|
295|**典型输出**：
296|```
297|结论: daemon 4 个工作线程全部在 pthread_mutex_lock 等待。
298|      gdb 显示 Thread 1 持有 lock A 等待 lock B，
299|      Thread 2 持有 lock B 等待 lock A——经典 ABBA 死锁。
300|根因: FUSE daemon 中锁获取顺序不一致，导致多线程死锁，
301|      文件系统操作完全挂起。
302|```
303|
304|#### Branch F — /dev/fuse 设备权限问题
305|
306|**触发条件**：容器或非 root 用户启动 FUSE daemon 时出现 Permission denied。
307|
308|```
309|L2 诊断：
310|├── 1. ls -la /dev/fuse（设备节点权限）
311|├── 2. getfacl /dev/fuse（ACL 权限检查）
312|├── 3. cat /proc/<daemon_pid>/status | grep Cap（daemon 能力集）
313|├── 4. grep fuse /etc/group（fuse 用户组）
314|├── 5. groups <daemon_user>（用户所属组）
315|├── 6. cat /etc/fuse.conf（FUSE 全局配置）
316|├── 7. capsh --print | grep fuse（进程能力检查）
317|├── 8. container environment: cat /proc/1/cgroup（容器内 cgroup 检查）
318|│
319|└── L3 根因判定：
320|    ├── /dev/fuse 权限 0600 root:root → 非 root 用户无法访问
321|    ├── daemon 用户不在 fuse 组 → 缺少 /dev/fuse 访问权限
322|    ├── 容器内未挂载 /dev/fuse → 设备节点不存在
323|    ├── 容器缺少 CAP_SYS_ADMIN 或 CAP_MKNOD → 无法操作 FUSE 设备
324|    ├── user_allow_other 未在 /etc/fuse.conf 启用 → 无法使用 allow_other
325|    ├── AppArmor/SELinux 阻止 FUSE 操作 → 安全策略限制
326|    └── daemon 进程 capabilities 被移除 → container runtime 降权
327|```
328|
329|**典型输出**：
330|```
331|结论: /dev/fuse 权限 0600 root:root，daemon 以非 root 用户
332|      运行且不在 fuse 用户组中。
333|      daemon 启动日志显示 "Permission denied" 打开 /dev/fuse。
334|根因: /dev/fuse 设备节点仅 root 可读写，FUSE daemon
335|      以普通用户运行且未加入 fuse 组，无法打开设备。
336|```
337|
338|#### Branch G — FUSE 内核模块 Bug
339|
340|**触发条件**：内核 Panic、Oops、soft lockup 与 FUSE 相关，或已知 FUSE 内核 Bug。
341|
342|```
343|L2 诊断：
344|├── 1. dmesg | grep -iE "fuse|libfuse"（内核 FUSE 消息）
345|├── 2. dmesg | grep -iE "kernel panic|Oops|BUG|soft lockup"（内核异常）
346|├── 3. cat /sys/module/fuse/version（FUSE 模块版本）
347|├── 4. uname -r（内核版本）
348|├── 5. cat /proc/self/mounts | grep fuse（所有 FUSE 挂载）
349|├── 6. cat /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/abort（abort 状态）
350|├── 7. test -f /var/crash/vmcore* 2>/dev/null && ls -lh /var/crash/（crash dump 检查）
351|├── 8. grep -i fuse /var/log/messages | tail -20（系统日志）
352|│
353|└── L3 根因判定：
354|    ├── 已知 FUSE 内核 Bug 列表匹配（CVE-xxxx-xxxx / 内核 commit）
355|    ├── 特定内核版本 + FUSE 版本组合已知不兼容
356|    ├── CR2 地址在 FUSE 模块区域内 → FUSE 内核模块导致 Panic
357|    ├── soft lockup 栈显示在 fuse_* 函数中 → FUSE 内核路径问题
358|    ├── 大规模并发操作触发的竞态条件 → 内核 FUSE 并发 Bug
359|    └── FUSE 模块参数不合理导致内核异常 → max_read 过小/过大
360|```
361|
362|**典型输出**：
363|```
364|结论: dmesg 显示 "kernel BUG at fs/fuse/dev.c:1234"，
365|      内核版本 5.15.0-rc3 存在已知 FUSE 并发访问 Bug。
366|      CR2 地址 0xffff888123456789 在 fuse_dev_do_write 函数范围内。
367|根因: 内核 FUSE 模块在特定内核版本下存在并发竞态条件，
368|      多线程并发写操作触发内核 BUG。
369|```
370|
371|#### Branch H — 混合/复杂 FUSE 故障
372|
373|**触发条件**：多种现象共存，或以上分支无法覆盖的复杂 FUSE 问题。
374|
375|```
376|L2 诊断：
377|├── 1. 执行所有以上分支的 L2 诊断（汇总所有证据）
378|├── 2. 交叉对比各分支症状（判定主次故障）
379|├── 3. 完整 strace -f -e trace=all -p <daemon_pid> -o /tmp/strace.log
380|├── 4. lsof -p <daemon_pid>（daemon 打开的文件/连接）
381|├── 5. tcpdump -i any host <backend_storage_ip>（后端存储网络抓包）
382|├── 6. strace -e trace=all ls -la <mount_point> 2>&1（客户端操作全追踪）
383|├── 7. 对比故障前后的 FUSE 配置快照（连接数、参数、daemon 版本）
384|│
385|└── L3 根因判定：
386|    ├── 按故障链优先级排序（先解决依赖的下层问题）
387|    ├── 多故障串联（daemon 崩溃 → 残留连接 → 新 daemon 无法挂载）
388|    ├── 配置错误叠加（max_read 过小 + 线程池太小 + writeback 未启用）
389|    ├── 环境变化触发（内核升级、cgroup 限制、SELinux 策略变更）
390|    └── 复杂的 libfuse API 使用错误（回调注册、会话管理、信号处理）
391|```
392|
393|**典型输出**：
394|```
395|结论: 多种故障共存：daemon 线程池过小（4 线程）导致写性能差，
396|      同时 max_read=4K 进一步退化读性能，writeback cache 启用
397|      但 daemon 未正确处理 ->write 回调。
398|根因: 多重配置叠加导致 FUSE 极端性能退化，建议逐一修复：
399|      1. 增大线程池至 16+
400|      2. 设置 max_read=128K+
401|      3. 检查 writeback cache 回调实现
402|```
403|
